synopsis: The manufacturer wants to validate most Collision Mitigation System behavior virtually, including establishing an existing-system baseline and comparing the new system in the same environments, but it has no current virtual-testing capability or prior experience with this validation [f6, f25, f26, f8258, f7512]. The programme has an eleven-month hard deadline, while the examined proposal allows four months to validate the new braking system; documented capability-building cases took years, and no single approach is documented as compressing validation from years to months [f9396, f10389, f1203, f308]. Simulation can multiply evidence and prioritize scarce prototype tests, but cannot certify perception alone; how much physical testing can safely be replaced remains uncertain, and sensor simulation can replace only part, not most, of physical sensor testing [f11311, f326, f5757, f4407]. No identified off-road document accepts simulation as compliance evidence or permits replacing prescribed physical tests, although ISO 18497-4:2024 was the closest off-road support found for simulation as a verification method; in contrast, 2025 supplements to UN Regulation No. 152 permit some virtual substitution for car and van AEBS [f2103, f5277, f7546]. Credibility rather than test volume is the central weakness: physical correlation is needed, dust remains the biggest off-road sensor-simulation gap, and no independent evidence supports purely virtual or HIL validation across 100+ site types and all relevant machines and environmental conditions without substantial real-world correlation [f10409, f8341, f4424, f5760]. For four-month validation, the recommended defensible route is an analytical safety case, targeted physical tests and simulation under a credibility framework, with closed-loop simulation required to capture braking-induced trajectory changes [f2137, f11322].

relations.note: Both state the manufacturer has no prior experience with this kind of virtual validation.
